\title{Label-Level Hierarchical Selective Acceptance of LLM Annotations with
Certified Error Control}

\author[zju,loctek]{Hongsheng Wang\corref{cor}}

\begin{abstract}
%ABSTRACT-BEGIN
Large language models (LLMs) routinely annotate items with hierarchical labels,
and deploying them means deciding which machine labels may enter a database
unreviewed. Existing selective-annotation methods decide per item: an item is
accepted with all its labels or reviewed in full. We study the label-level
problem and propose \hlcl{}. It scores each predicted node from the agreement
of repeated LLM samples and sibling competition, accepts a prefix of each
predicted path so that accepted labels are ancestor-closed, and certifies one
threshold per depth with a learn-then-test procedure. The certificate bounds
the label-level error ratio (wrong accepted labels over accepted labels) with
probability $1-\delta$, needs only i.i.d.\ items, and uses a pooled betting test
or an exact depth-wise test chosen on held-out data. Among certified thresholds, \hlcl{} deploys the one with the
lowest human effort under an explicit cost model. On four public taxonomies
of depth two to four, two LLM annotators and 100 splits per setting, the realised
error exceeded the target in at most \stat{s@maxviol@HLCL} of splits. Compared
with an item-level rule under the same certificate, deciding per label raised
the share of correct labels accepted without review from
\res{bgc}{0.05}{ItemBest}{power} to \res{bgc}{0.05}{HLCL}{power} on the Blurb
Genre Collection at $\alpha=0.05$. Against the strongest certified baseline in
each setting, \hlcl{} had lower mean effort in \stat{s@lowermean} of
\stat{s@nsettings} settings; after correcting for overlapping splits it is
significantly cheaper in \stat{s@wins}, significantly more expensive in
\stat{s@losses}, and not significantly different in the rest.
%ABSTRACT-END
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Labelled data is the scarcest input of most knowledge-intensive systems, and
the labelling step is where their quality is decided. Human annotation is
accurate but slow, and large language models (LLMs) have become a default
first-pass annotator: they are cheap, available at scale, and on many taxonomic
tasks they agree with human annotators often enough to be useful. Their errors,
however, are not uniform. An LLM is typically sure about the coarse category of
an item and unsure about the fine one: asking it to tag an abstract as
\emph{Medicine} is usually safe, asking it to choose among dozens of medical
sub-disciplines is not. A practitioner who deploys such an annotator therefore
faces a per-label decision: \emph{which parts of the machine output can be
written into the database without review, and which must be confirmed by a
person?}

Two constraints shape the answer. The first is a \emph{quality target}: the
labels written without review must be right to within a specified error rate
$\alpha$, because they enter downstream aggregations that nobody will audit
again. The second is a \emph{reviewing budget}: human attention is the resource
being saved, and a procedure that certifies a threshold but routes most of the
corpus to reviewers has not solved the problem.

Selective annotation addresses the first constraint. Conformal labeling
\cite{huang2025selective} builds a conformal $p$-value for each item and applies
the Benjamini--Hochberg procedure to control the false discovery rate (FDR) of
the items whose machine labels are kept; conformal alignment
\cite{gui2024conformalalignment} and selection with conformal $p$-values
\cite{jin2023selection} give related guarantees, and budget-aware routing
\cite{jung2025trust,quorum2026} addresses the second constraint. These methods
share a structural assumption that does not fit hierarchical annotation: the
unit of decision is the \emph{item}. An item whose coarse label is certain and
whose fine label is a coin flip is either accepted in full, admitting the error,
or reviewed in full, paying for work that was only needed one level down. The
cost of this granularity can be large. On the Blurb Genre Collection at
$\alpha=0.05$, an item-level rule with exactly our certificate accepts at most
\res{bgc}{0.05}{ItemBest}{power} of the correct labels without review (with the
better of its test choices); deciding per label accepts
\res{bgc}{0.05}{HLCL}{power} (\S\ref{sec:exp-results}).

Moving to labels raises two difficulties. The first is statistical. Labels of
one item are predicted from the same text and are dependent, and a hierarchy
adds dependence between a node and its descendants; a procedure that treats
labels as exchangeable units has no guarantee for the label-level ratio, and
reusing calibration data to fit the score that is then tested is known to break
selective-risk guarantees \cite{perfield2026}. The second difficulty is structural: a label-level rule that
ignores the taxonomy may accept a fine label while rejecting its parent, which
yields a label set that is not a path and that downstream systems cannot store.

\paragraph{Contributions}
\begin{enumerate}
  \item We formulate \emph{label-level hierarchical selective acceptance}: for
  every predicted node, decide accept or review, subject to a high-probability
  bound on the label-level FDR, with an explicit model of human effort as the
  objective (\S\ref{sec:setting}).
  \item We propose \hlcl{}, which combines standard tools for this problem: a
  node score built from sample agreement and from sibling competition, an
  ancestor-closed acceptance rule with one threshold per depth, and a
  learn-then-test
  calibration in which the candidate thresholds, their order and the test
  statistic are all fixed on data disjoint from the calibration split
  (\S\ref{sec:method}). With a single shared threshold, the rule coincides with
  that of hierarchical selective classification \cite{goren2024hierarchical};
  what changes is the certified quantity.
  \item We show that the deployed rule satisfies the label-level bound with
  probability at least $1-\delta$ when items are i.i.d., with no assumption on
  the dependence between labels of the same item. Because the label-level ratio
  is a weighted average of per-depth rates, an exact depth-wise
  intersection--union test is available; it remains usable when $\alpha$ is
  small (\S\ref{sec:method-cert}, \ref{app:proofs}).
  \item We evaluate on four public hierarchical corpora of depth two to four
  with two LLM annotators and 100 random splits per setting, against six baselines,
  ablations under a fixed test statistic, and sensitivity to the review
  overhead, the calibration size and $\delta$. Wins and losses are decided by
  paired confidence intervals corrected for overlapping splits, and we report
  where \hlcl{} does not help (\S\ref{sec:exp}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Problem setting}
\label{sec:setting}

\subsection{Hierarchical labels and annotators}

Let $\mathcal{T}$ be a label taxonomy, a rooted tree whose nodes are labels and
whose root-to-leaf paths have length at most $D$. An \emph{item} is a text
$x_i$, and its gold annotation is a path $(y^\star_{i,1},\dots,y^\star_{i,d_i})$
with one node per depth, so every ancestor of a gold node is also gold. This
ancestor closure is the convention of hierarchical corpora such as RCV1
\cite{lewis2004rcv1}, Web of Science and the Blurb Genre Collection.

An annotator maps $x_i$ to a predicted path
$(\hat y_{i,1},\dots,\hat y_{i,\hat d_i})$. In this paper it is an LLM queried
$k$ times with temperature sampling, but the method only needs a score for every
predicted node. A predicted node at depth $d$ is \emph{correct} if the
prediction agrees with the gold path up to depth $d$; a wrong fine label is
therefore an error even when the coarse label is right.

A decision rule with parameters $\lambda$ accepts some predicted nodes. Let
$A(\lambda)$ and $W(\lambda)$ be the numbers of accepted and of accepted-and-wrong
nodes of a random item. We define the label-level false discovery rate as the
ratio of expectations (a marginal FDR, \emph{mFDR})
\begin{equation}
  \fdr(\lambda) \;=\; \frac{\E[W(\lambda)]}{\E[A(\lambda)]},
  \label{eq:fdr}
\end{equation}
the long-run share of wrong labels among the labels written without review,
with the convention $\fdr(\lambda)=0$ when $\E[A(\lambda)]=0$ (a rule that
accepts nothing makes no error). The node score is fitted on separate data
(\S\ref{sec:method-score}) and is treated as fixed, so \eqref{eq:fdr} is
defined conditionally on the fitted score. This is the quantity an operator
monitors, and it does not require labels of the same item to be independent.

\paragraph{Form of the guarantee}
The rule is chosen from a labelled calibration sample, so $\fdr(\hat\lambda)$ is
a random quantity. We ask that
\begin{equation}
  \Pr\bigl(\fdr(\hat\lambda) \le \alpha\bigr) \;\ge\; 1-\delta ,
  \label{eq:guarantee}
\end{equation}
with the probability taken over the calibration sample. Conformal labeling
\cite{huang2025selective} instead controls the expected false discovery
proportion $\E[\mathrm{FDP}]$ over calibration and test draws. The two
guarantees bound different functionals and neither implies the other: ours
fixes the target functional (the population ratio \eqref{eq:fdr}) and
guarantees that the \emph{deployed} rule meets it with probability $1-\delta$;
theirs averages the realised proportion over repetitions. The high-probability
form suits an operator who must vouch for one released dataset; we compare the
two empirically in \S\ref{sec:exp-results}.

\subsection{Human effort}

Reviewing an item does not have a fixed cost: a reviewer who is told that the
coarse label is certified and only chooses the sub-category does less work than
one who annotates the item from scratch. Let $A_{i,d}\in\{0,1\}$ indicate that
the depth-$d$ node of item $i$ was accepted. The cost of item $i$ is
\begin{equation}
  c_i \;=\; \sum_{d=1}^{D} \omega_d\,\mathbf{1}\{A_{i,d}=0\}
  \;+\; c_0\,\mathbf{1}\{\exists d: A_{i,d}=0\},
  \label{eq:effort}
\end{equation}
where $\omega_d\ge0$ with $\sum_d \omega_d=1$ is the share of a full annotation spent on
level $d$, and $c_0$ is a fixed overhead for opening and reading an item. A
fully accepted item costs $0$ and a fully manual one costs $1+c_0$. We report
effort as $\E[c]/(1+c_0)$, the fraction of the cost of annotating the corpus by
hand. The overhead matters: without it, the cheapest rule would touch nearly
every item to fix only its fine level. We use $c_0=0.5$ and equal $\omega_d$ and
vary $c_0$ in \S\ref{sec:exp-sens}. Neither value comes from a timing study;
they are a transparent default, and the sensitivity analysis shows that the
guarantee does not depend on them and the ranking of methods changes little.

\subsection{Objective}

For a risk level $\alpha$ and a confidence $1-\delta$ we seek
\begin{equation}
  \hat\lambda \in \argmin_{\lambda}\; \E[c(\lambda)]
  \quad\text{subject to \eqref{eq:guarantee}.}
  \label{eq:objective}
\end{equation}
The decision is made per node, so a rule may accept the coarse level of an item
and route only its finer levels. The constraint is on the pooled label-level
ratio, which is weaker, and hence easier to meet, than bounding every depth
separately.

\begin{definition}[Ancestor closure]
\label{def:closure}
A decision rule is \emph{ancestor-closed} if it accepts a node only when it
accepts all predicted ancestors of that node.
\end{definition}

Closure is required for the output to be usable. A label set that contains a
fine label without its parent is not a path in $\mathcal{T}$: it cannot be
stored in a path-keyed table and fails any taxonomy validator. Closure also
matches the task: if the annotator hesitates between \emph{Cardiology} and
\emph{Neurology}, the useful partial output is the certified parent
\emph{Medicine}.

\section{Related work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Selective annotation with guarantees}
Huang et al.~\cite{huang2025selective} propose conformal labeling: a conformal
$p$-value per item, computed against calibration items that the model
mislabelled, followed by Benjamini--Hochberg at level $\alpha$, controls the
expected FDR of the set of items whose machine labels are used. Gui et
al.~\cite{gui2024conformalalignment} apply the same construction to decide when
the output of a foundation model can be trusted, and Jin and
Cand\`es~\cite{jin2023selection} develop the underlying theory of selection with
conformal $p$-values. All three select whole items and assume one label per
item. \hlcl{} differs in the unit of decision, in enforcing ancestor closure and
in the form of the guarantee.

\paragraph{Routing between humans and models}
Jung et al.~\cite{jung2025trust} decide when an LLM judge should defer to a
human, using learn-then-test to bound disagreement with human judgments.
Purificato et al.~\cite{quorum2026} route instances to human or LLM annotators
under a budget using difficulty features, without a statistical guarantee. Both
decide per item and address how review capacity is spent; they can be combined
with \hlcl{}, which decides what needs review in the first place.

\paragraph{Selective and hierarchical selective classification}
Selective classification lets a classifier abstain; Geifman and
El-Yaniv~\cite{geifman2017selective} give a threshold rule with a
high-probability bound on the risk of the accepted predictions, the direct
ancestor of our item-level certified baseline. Goren et al.~\cite{goren2024hierarchical}
extend this to hierarchies: instead of abstaining, the classifier backs off to an
ancestor of its prediction, and a threshold is calibrated so that the returned
nodes meet a target accuracy with high probability. This is the closest work to
ours and our ancestor-closed rule has the same shape. The differences are in the
target and the decision. Hierarchical selective classification bounds the error
of the returned node over all items, including items that back off to the root,
and chooses the threshold that returns the most specific nodes; we bound the
error among the labels written without review (a false discovery rate), certify
a separate threshold per depth with two complementary tests, and choose among
certified thresholds by human effort. We include an adaptation of it as a
baseline (\S\ref{sec:exp-base}). Surveys of hierarchical classification
\cite{silla2011survey} describe the top-down, per-level decision structure that
our rule inherits.

\paragraph{Guarantees below the item}
Mohri and Hashimoto~\cite{mohri2024language} remove claims from a generated text
until the remainder is certified factual, a back-off close in spirit to our
ancestor closure; the unit is a claim rather than a taxonomy node, and there is
no budget. Gurram~\cite{perfield2026} controls the selective risk per field in
document extraction, the label-level granularity we adopt, and documents how
score refitting and clustering of fields within a document invalidate naive
procedures. Fields of a form are not organised in a hierarchy, and that work
does not accept a coarse unit while routing a fine one; we use its field-level
procedure as a baseline. Hierarchical conformal classification
\cite{denhengst2025hierarchical,mortier2025conformal} and tree-based conformal
prediction for multi-label data \cite{tyagi2023multilabel} return mixed-level
prediction sets with coverage guarantees. Coverage asks that the truth lie in
the returned set; we ask that the labels written without review be right, which
is a different requirement, and none of these methods models human effort.

\paragraph{LLM annotations in statistical inference}
Prediction-powered inference \cite{angelopoulos2023ppi} and its use with LLM
annotations \cite{gligoric2025unconfident} combine many machine labels with a
few human labels to obtain valid confidence intervals for population quantities.
Their goal is an estimate, not a per-item decision about which labels to keep;
they are complementary to \hlcl{}, which decides which labels can be stored.

\paragraph{Calibration}
Post-hoc calibration such as temperature scaling \cite{guo2017calibration}
improves the reliability of confidence scores. A calibrated score still leaves
open where to cut, and the cut must be justified on labelled data; \hlcl{} does
not need its score to be calibrated for the guarantee to hold.

\paragraph{Learn-then-test and betting tests}
Our calibration is an instance of learn-then-test \cite{angelopoulos2025learnthen}:
candidate parameters are hypotheses tested in a fixed sequence
\cite{bauer1991multiple}, which controls the family-wise error rate without
splitting the error budget across candidates. We use the betting $p$-values of
Waudby-Smith and Ramdas~\cite{waudbysmith2024estimating}. Conformal risk control
\cite{angelopoulos2024conformal} bounds an expected monotone loss and could
replace our certificate when an expectation guarantee suffices. The individual
statistical tools we use are standard. What is specific to our setting is the
hypothesis family (per-depth thresholds under ancestor closure), the observation
that the label-level ratio is a weighted average of per-depth rates, which makes
an exact intersection--union test available, the selection between the two tests
on held-out data, and the effort-based choice among certified thresholds. We
regard the formulation and its evaluation, rather than any single tool, as the
contribution.

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}

\hlcl{} has four parts: a node score (\S\ref{sec:method-score}), an
ancestor-closed acceptance rule (\S\ref{sec:method-rule}), a certificate
(\S\ref{sec:method-cert}) and the choice of the deployed threshold
(\S\ref{sec:method-select}). Algorithm~\ref{alg:hlcl} summarises the procedure.

\subsection{Node score from repeated annotation}
\label{sec:method-score}

The annotator is queried $k$ times with temperature sampling and asked for one
path and a stated confidence per level. At each depth, the $k$ paths that agree
with the prefix chosen so far define a distribution over candidate nodes, and
the \emph{consensus path} follows its mode. A node $v$ at depth $d$ is described
by
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{vote}: the share of the $k$ samples whose path agrees with the
  consensus up to $v$; this is non-increasing along a path;
  \item \textbf{conditional agreement}: $\mathrm{vote}(v)/\mathrm{vote}(\mathrm{parent}(v))$;
  \item \textbf{sibling margin and entropy}: the gap between the two largest
  conditional shares at depth $d$ and the entropy of the conditional
  distribution;
  \item \textbf{stated confidence}: mean and standard deviation of the
  confidence the annotator reports for this level over the supporting samples;
  \item the parent's vote, the logarithm of the parent's fan-out in
  $\mathcal{T}$, and a depth indicator.
\end{itemize}
A logistic regression on these features, fitted on a \emph{fit split} that is
disjoint from the calibration and test data, maps each node to a score
$s\in(0,1)$. Unlike the vote, $s$ is not monotone along a path, because a child
can face weaker competition than its parent. Ancestor closure is therefore a
real constraint on the rule. Keeping the fit split separate prevents the
score-refit leakage described in \cite{perfield2026}.

\subsection{Acceptance rule}
\label{sec:method-rule}

Given thresholds $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_D)$, one per depth, the rule
accepts the depth-$d$ node of item $i$ when
\begin{equation}
  A_{i,d} \;=\; \prod_{e\le d}\mathbf{1}\{s_{i,e}\ge\lambda_e\}=1,
  \label{eq:rule}
\end{equation}
where $s_{i,e}$ is the score of the node of item $i$ at depth $e$. The accepted
set of every item is a prefix of its predicted path and hence ancestor-closed
(\ref{app:proofs}). A reviewer of a partially accepted item receives the
certified prefix and decides only the remaining levels, which is the cost model
\eqref{eq:effort}.

We use one threshold per depth rather than one per node. A per-node rule has as
many parameters as $\mathcal{T}$ has nodes and cannot be certified from a
calibration sample of realistic size; a per-depth rule has $D$ parameters and is
unaffected by adding leaves at an existing depth. The candidate set contains
the grid of per-depth threshold vectors built from score quantiles on the fit
split and, as a special case, the vectors with equal thresholds at all depths.

\subsection{Certificate}
\label{sec:method-cert}

For item $i$ let $A_i(\lambda)=\sum_d A_{i,d}$ and
$W_i(\lambda)=\sum_d A_{i,d}\mathbf{1}\{C_{i,d}=0\}$, where $C_{i,d}$ indicates
that the node is correct, and define the loss
\begin{equation}
  L_i(\lambda) \;=\; W_i(\lambda)-\alpha A_i(\lambda)\;\in\;[-\alpha D,\,(1-\alpha)D].
  \label{eq:loss}
\end{equation}
If items are i.i.d., so are $L_1(\lambda),\dots,L_n(\lambda)$, and
\begin{equation}
  \E[L(\lambda)]\le 0 \iff \E[W(\lambda)]\le\alpha\,\E[A(\lambda)]
  \iff \fdr(\lambda)\le\alpha
  \label{eq:equiv}
\end{equation}
whenever $\E[A(\lambda)]>0$. A valid $p$-value for the null
$H_\lambda:\fdr(\lambda)>\alpha$ is therefore all that is needed. The labels of
one item may be arbitrarily dependent, because each item contributes one scalar
$L_i$.

\paragraph{Pooled betting test}
Rescale $L$ to $x\in[0,1]$ and let $t$ be the rescaled zero. Under $H_\lambda$,
$\E[x]>t$, and the capital
$K_m=\prod_{i\le m}\bigl(1+\ell_i(t-x_i)\bigr)$ with predictable bets
$\ell_i\in[0,\,0.5/(1-t)]$ is a nonnegative supermartingale, so
$p^{\mathrm{bet}}=1/\max_m K_m$ is a valid $p$-value by Ville's inequality
\cite{waudbysmith2024estimating}. We use the predictable plug-in bet
$\ell_i=\min\{\sqrt{2\log(20)/(n\hat\sigma^2_{i-1})},\,0.5/(1-t)\}$, where
$\hat\sigma^2_{i-1}$ is a regularised running variance of $x_1,\dots,x_{i-1}$
and the items are visited in a fixed random order; the bet adapts to the small
variance of $L$ at conservative thresholds. Any predictable bet in the stated
range gives a valid $p$-value.

\paragraph{Depth-wise intersection--union test}
Let $q_d=\E[W_d]/\E[A_d]$ be the error rate among nodes accepted at depth $d$.
The pooled rate is a weighted average of these,
\begin{equation}
  \fdr(\lambda)=\frac{\sum_d\E[W_d]}{\sum_d\E[A_d]}
  =\sum_d\frac{\E[A_d]}{\sum_e\E[A_e]}\,q_d ,
  \label{eq:weightedavg}
\end{equation}
so $\fdr(\lambda)>\alpha$ implies $q_d>\alpha$ for some $d$, i.e.\
$H_\lambda\subseteq\bigcup_d H_d$ with $H_d:q_d>\alpha$. Because the pairs
$(A_{i,d},W_{i,d})$ are i.i.d.\ across items, conditionally on which items are
accepted at depth $d$ their error indicators are independent with success
probability $q_d$. With $n_d$ acceptances and $w_d$ errors,
\begin{equation}
  p_d=\Pr\bigl(\Bin(n_d,\alpha)\le w_d\bigr)
  \label{eq:binomial}
\end{equation}
is an exact $p$-value for $H_d$; if a depth has a finite threshold but no
acceptance in the sample we set $p_d=1$, and depths with an infinite threshold
are omitted. By the intersection--union principle,
\begin{equation}
  p^{\mathrm{iut}}=\max_d p_d
  \label{eq:iut}
\end{equation}
is a valid $p$-value for $H_\lambda$ without multiplicity correction
(\ref{app:proofs}). The test depends on the score only through which nodes are
accepted. It is coarser than the pooled test, since it asks every depth to meet
$\alpha$, but it uses exact tails and remains usable when $\alpha n$ is small.

\paragraph{Choosing the test}
Neither test dominates the other: the pooled test exploits the constraint that
is actually the target and is sharper when depths differ in error rate, while
the depth-wise test is the only one that certifies anything when $\alpha$ is
very small. \hlcl{} uses the pooled test if, on the fit split, the sequence it
induces certifies at least one candidate, and the depth-wise test otherwise.
The rule depends only on the fit split, so it does not affect the guarantee.
The fit-split scores used for these decisions are in-sample (the score was
trained on the same items), which makes the rule slightly optimistic; we tried
two-fold cross-fitting instead and found it made the candidate order worse, not
better, because each half-model is trained on half as many items (in a pilot on
DBPedia, effort at $\alpha=0.1$ rose from $0.00$ to $0.06$). We therefore keep
the in-sample variant; either choice is valid.

\begin{theorem}[Validity]
\label{thm:validity}
Assume the fit, calibration and test items are i.i.d. Let the candidate set,
their order and the choice of test be measurable functions of the fit split,
and let candidates be tested on the calibration split in that order, stopping at
the first $p$-value above $\delta$. Then, with probability at least $1-\delta$
over the calibration split and conditionally on the fit split, every certified
candidate $\lambda$ satisfies $\fdr(\lambda)\le\alpha$. In particular the
deployed $\hat\lambda$ satisfies \eqref{eq:guarantee}.
\end{theorem}

The proof is in \ref{app:proofs}. The guarantee is about the deployed rule: any
selection among certified candidates, including the effort criterion below,
preserves it, because all of them are covered simultaneously.

\subsection{Choosing the deployed threshold}
\label{sec:method-select}

Certification leaves a set of admissible thresholds. Selective annotation
methods usually deploy the most permissive one, which maximises the number of
accepted labels. \hlcl{} instead estimates the effort \eqref{eq:effort} of each
certified candidate on the calibration split and deploys the cheapest. The two
criteria differ when a threshold accepts slightly more labels but leaves more
items partially open, each of which pays the overhead $c_0$.

\begin{algorithm}[t]
\caption{\hlcl{}}
\label{alg:hlcl}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\Require items, annotator, taxonomy $\mathcal{T}$, risk $\alpha$, confidence
$\delta$, cost model $(\omega,c_0)$
\State query the annotator $k$ times per item; build consensus paths and node features
\State split the labelled items into fit, calibration and test parts
\State fit the node score $s$ on the fit split
\State build candidate threshold vectors from score quantiles on the fit split
\State choose the test statistic on the fit split (\S\ref{sec:method-cert})
\State order candidates by their $p$-value on the fit split, conservative first among ties
\For{each candidate $\lambda$ in this order}
  \State compute its $p$-value on the calibration split
  \If{$p>\delta$} \textbf{break}
  \EndIf
  \State record $\lambda$ and its estimated effort $\hat c(\lambda)$
\EndFor
\State \Return the recorded $\lambda$ with the smallest $\hat c$ (accept nothing if none)
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:exp}

\subsection{Data and annotators}
\label{sec:exp-data}

We use four public hierarchical corpora whose fine levels differ in difficulty:
DBPedia classes ($9/70/219$ labels at three levels), WOS-46985 ($7/134$ labels at
two levels), the Blurb Genre Collection (three levels, 147-edge official
hierarchy; we keep the blurbs whose genre path is unique and has at least three
levels) and the Home \& Kitchen product categories of Amazon Reviews 2023
\cite{hou2024amazon} (four levels, $8/31/112/296$ nodes; from the first 400,000
records of the metadata file we keep products whose category path has at least
four levels below the root and paths with at least 100 products, a pool of
154,787 products, and use the title, the first 500 characters of the features
and the first 400 of the description, truncated to 1,200 characters, as text). From each we draw $3{,}000$ items with a fixed seed.
Annotator A (\texttt{deepseek-chat}) labels all four corpora; annotator B
(\texttt{claude-haiku-4-5}), from a different model family, labels the Blurb
collection again. Each item is queried $k=5$ times at temperature $1.0$. All
75,000 responses are cached and released, so every number below can be
reproduced without API access. Four responses could not be parsed (three
blank ones on WOS-46985 and one truncated one from annotator B) and count as
missing samples; on Amazon, three responses left every level empty and count
as votes for no label.

Table~\ref{tab:annot} gives the per-depth accuracy of the consensus path.
DBPedia is easy at every level; the Blurb collection degrades at the third
level, more for annotator B; Amazon degrades steadily with depth, from
$0.97$ at the first level to $0.73$ at the fourth;
WOS-46985 is hard at the second level, where the
annotator is right less than half the time. In that regime no certified method
can accept much at small $\alpha$, and we report it as such.

\subsection{Baselines}
\label{sec:exp-base}

All methods use the same learned node score $s$ and the same splits.
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Item-level certified selection} (Item-cert.): each item is
  scored by its weakest node and one threshold is certified, so the item is
  accepted or reviewed as a whole. This is the high-probability selective rule
  of \cite{geifman2017selective} applied to items, with our certificate. We run
  it with the automatic test choice of \hlcl{}, with the pooled test only and
  with the depth-wise test only, and in every table report the variant with the
  lowest mean effort in that setting (Item-cert.$^\ast$). Choosing this variant
  on the test results is an oracle choice that can only favour the baseline.
  \item \textbf{Hierarchical selective classification} (HSC)
  \cite{goren2024hierarchical}: each item returns the deepest prefix of its
  predicted path whose nodes all clear one shared threshold. The original method
  scores a node by the aggregated probability of its descendants under a
  flat classifier; we use our node score instead, so that all methods share
  one score. Following that
  work, the risk is the item-level error over all items (an item backed off to
  the root counts as correct), certified with an exact binomial tail and fixed
  sequence testing, and the most permissive certified threshold is deployed.
  Its guarantee is thus on a different quantity from ours; we report it because
  it is the closest published hierarchical back-off method.
  \item \textbf{Per-field selective risk control} (Per-field)
  \cite{perfield2026}: one threshold per depth, certified with an exact binomial
  tail at level $\delta/D$ (Bonferroni over depths), as in the field-i.i.d.\
  tier of that work. Candidate thresholds and their order come from the fit
  split; the most permissive certified threshold is deployed. Depths are treated
  as independent fields and closure is not enforced.
  \item \textbf{Item-level conformal selection} (Item-conf.)
  \cite{huang2025selective,jin2023selection}: a conformal $p$-value per item from
  the item score, followed by Benjamini--Hochberg at level $\alpha$. It controls
  the \emph{expected} item-level FDR, which upper-bounds the expected label-level
  FDR, but does not give \eqref{eq:guarantee}. It does not use the fit split.
  \item \textbf{Depth-wise Benjamini--Hochberg} (Depth-BH): conformal $p$-values
  per node and Benjamini--Hochberg separately at each depth. Nodes of one depth
  are i.i.d.\ across items, so this controls the expected FDP at each depth; it
  gives no high-probability statement and no direct statement about the pooled
  ratio.
  \item \textbf{Fixed threshold} ($s\ge0.9$): the common practitioner rule, with
  no guarantee.
\end{itemize}
Item-cert., HSC and Per-field carry high-probability certificates; we call them
the \emph{certified baselines}. Item-conf.\ and Depth-BH carry expected-value
guarantees.

\subsection{Protocol}
\label{sec:exp-proto}

For each corpus, annotator and $\alpha$ we draw 100 random splits into fit,
calibration and test parts (600/1200/1200 items). The score, the candidates,
their order and the test statistic are fixed on the fit split, certification
uses the calibration split only, and all reported numbers are computed on the
test split with $\delta=0.1$ unless stated otherwise. We report (i)
\emph{power}, the share of correct label nodes accepted without review; (ii)
\emph{effort} \eqref{eq:effort} as a fraction of fully manual annotation; and
(iii) \emph{viol.}, the share of splits whose realised label-level error on the
test split exceeds $\alpha$. The guarantee concerns the population rate, so
viol.\ also counts test-sample fluctuations and is a conservative check: a valid
method should stay near or below $\delta=0.1$. The values of $\alpha$ differ by
corpus because a useful range depends on the annotator's accuracy.

To compare two methods in a setting we use the paired difference of their effort
over the 100 splits. The splits are drawn from the same 3,000 items, so the
differences are positively correlated and the naive standard error is too
small; we therefore use the corrected resampled-$t$ variance of Nadeau and
Bengio~\cite{nadeau2003inference}, which multiplies the sample variance by
$1/J+n_{\mathrm{test}}/n_{\mathrm{train}}=\stat{s@nbfactor}$ (with $J=100$
splits, $n_{\mathrm{test}}=1200$, $n_{\mathrm{train}}=1800$). \hlcl{}
\emph{wins} a setting if the corrected 95\% interval for (\hlcl{} $-$ baseline)
lies below zero, \emph{loses} if it lies above zero, and \emph{ties}
otherwise.

\begin{figure*}[t]

Table~\ref{tab:main} and Figures~\ref{fig:power}--\ref{fig:validity} summarise
the results.

\paragraph{Validity}
The realised error of \hlcl{} exceeded $\alpha$ in at most
\stat{s@maxviol@HLCL} of splits in any setting, consistent with $\delta=0.1$
(Figure~\ref{fig:validity}); so did Item-cert.\ (\stat{s@maxviol@ItemBest}) and
Per-field (\stat{s@maxviol@PerField-LTT}). HSC certifies the item-level error
over all items, a different quantity, and when the annotator is weak its
label-level error among accepted labels can be far above $\alpha$: on WOS-46985
at $\alpha=0.1$ it exceeded $\alpha$ in \res{wos}{0.1}{HSC}{viol} of splits,
because over a third of the items back off to the root, count as correct, and
leave room for errors among the accepted labels. HSC is therefore treated as a valid
competitor only in the rows where it met the label-level target. Depth-wise
Benjamini--Hochberg exceeded $\alpha$ in up to \stat{s@maxviol@DepthBH} of
splits although its mean realised error stays close to $\alpha$ (at most
\stat{s@maxfdpratio@DepthBH}$\,\alpha$): this is what an expected-value
guarantee at the boundary looks like, not a failure of the method. The fixed
threshold exceeded $\alpha$ in up to \stat{s@maxviol@Conf>=0.9} of splits (on
WOS-46985 it accepts labels with an error rate of \stat{s@wosfdpconf}), and
item-level conformal selection in up to \stat{s@maxviol@ConfLabel}.

\paragraph{Unit of decision}
Item-cert.\ carries exactly the certificate of \hlcl{}; we report its best test
choice per setting, so the comparison isolates the unit of decision and, if
anything, favours the baseline. At moderate risk, deciding per label accepts
more correct labels: on the Blurb collection at $\alpha=0.05$,
\res{bgc}{0.05}{HLCL}{power} against \res{bgc}{0.05}{ItemBest}{power} for
annotator A and \res{bgc_haiku}{0.05}{HLCL}{power} against
\res{bgc_haiku}{0.05}{ItemBest}{power} for annotator B; on WOS-46985 at
$\alpha=0.2$, \res{wos}{0.2}{HLCL}{power} against \res{wos}{0.2}{ItemBest}{power};
and on the four-level Amazon taxonomy at $\alpha=0.05$,
\res{amazon}{0.05}{HLCL}{power} against \res{amazon}{0.05}{ItemBest}{power}.
The gap shrinks as $\alpha$ grows (\res{bgc}{0.1}{HLCL}{power} against
\res{bgc}{0.1}{ItemBest}{power} on the Blurb collection at $\alpha=0.1$), and
close to the annotator's own error rate both rules accept almost everything;
the item-level rule can then be slightly cheaper because it leaves no item
partially open (DBPedia at $\alpha=0.05$: paired difference \hlcl{} $-$
Item-cert.\ \res{dbpedia}{0.05}{best}{dif}).

\paragraph{Effort against the strongest certified baseline}
In each setting we compare \hlcl{} with whichever valid certified baseline has
the lowest mean effort (Table~\ref{tab:main}). \hlcl{} has the lower mean effort
in \stat{s@lowermean} of the \stat{s@nsettings} settings. With the
Nadeau--Bengio correction \hlcl{} is significantly cheaper in \stat{s@wins}
settings: on the Blurb collection against HSC at $\alpha=0.05$
(\res{bgc}{0.05}{best}{dif}) and against Item-cert.\ at $\alpha=0.1$
(\res{bgc}{0.1}{best}{dif}), and on Amazon against HSC at $\alpha=0.05$
(\res{amazon}{0.05}{best}{dif}); there \hlcl{} was cheaper in
\res{bgc}{0.05}{best}{winshare}, \res{bgc}{0.1}{best}{winshare} and
\res{amazon}{0.05}{best}{winshare} of the splits. It is significantly more
expensive in \stat{s@losses} setting, Amazon at $\alpha=0.02$, against HSC
(\res{amazon}{0.02}{best}{dif}). In the remaining \stat{s@ties} settings the
corrected intervals include zero. The largest of these are in favour of \hlcl{} (WOS-46985 at $\alpha=0.2$:
\res{wos}{0.2}{best}{dif}, cheaper in \res{wos}{0.2}{best}{winshare} of splits;
at $\alpha=0.3$: \res{wos}{0.3}{best}{dif}), and the largest against it are
DBPedia at $\alpha=0.01$ (\res{dbpedia}{0.01}{best}{dif}) and the Blurb
collection at $\alpha=0.02$ (\res{bgc}{0.02}{best}{dif}), both against HSC. The
correction is conservative; we report it because the splits overlap and a
naive interval would overstate significance.

\paragraph{Where \hlcl{} does not help}
Three regimes stand out. First, at the smallest $\alpha$ on DBPedia, the
Blurb collection and Amazon, HSC is cheaper, significantly so on Amazon. There \hlcl{} must use the depth-wise test,
because the pooled test certifies little (on Amazon a non-empty rule in under
half of the splits), and the depth-wise test asks every
depth to meet $\alpha$; HSC bounds the item-level error over all items, which is
easier to meet when almost every item has a correct coarse label. Its mean
label-level error stayed below $\alpha$ in these settings, although it exceeded
$\alpha$ in \res{dbpedia}{0.01}{HSC}{viol} of splits on DBPedia. We cannot tell
from these data whether the conservativeness of the depth-wise certificate or the
label-level target itself is the main cause: the pooled test, which targets the
same ratio, certifies little there either (effort
\res{amazon}{0.02}{HLCL-wsr}{effort} on Amazon). Second, when $\alpha$ is close to the annotator's
error rate, the item-level rule with the same certificate is as cheap or cheaper
(DBPedia at $\alpha=0.05$). Third, on DBPedia at $\alpha=0.02$ item-level
conformal selection, which controls only an expectation, is the cheapest method
among those that met the target (\res{dbpedia}{0.02}{ConfLabel}{effort} against
\res{dbpedia}{0.02}{HLCL}{effort}); at $\alpha=0.01$ it exceeded $\alpha$ in
\res{dbpedia}{0.01}{ConfLabel}{viol} of splits.

\subsection{Ablations}
\label{sec:exp-abl}

\begin{table*}[t]
\centering
\scriptsize
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{2pt}
\caption{Effort of \hlcl{} variants (100 splits; lower is better; bold: within
$0.005$ of the best in the row and test group). Each variant is run with the
automatic choice of test (left), with the pooled betting test only (middle) and
with the depth-wise test only (right), so that the effect of a component is not
confounded with the test that happens to be selected. \emph{vote}: raw sample
agreement instead of the learned score; \emph{no cl.}: no ancestor closure,
nodes accepted independently; \emph{tied}: one threshold for all depths.}
\label{tab:abl}
\input{tables/ablations}
\end{table*}

Table~\ref{tab:abl} varies one component at a time under a fixed test.

\paragraph{Test statistic}
The test has by far the largest effect. With the pooled test only, \hlcl{}
certifies almost nothing at the smallest $\alpha$ (effort
\res{dbpedia}{0.01}{HLCL-wsr}{effort} on DBPedia at $\alpha=0.01$,
\res{bgc}{0.02}{HLCL-wsr}{effort} on the Blurb collection at $\alpha=0.02$);
with the depth-wise test only, it is much more expensive at larger $\alpha$
(\res{bgc}{0.1}{HLCL-iut}{effort} against \res{bgc}{0.1}{HLCL-wsr}{effort} on
the Blurb collection at $\alpha=0.1$). The selection rule picked the depth-wise
test in all or nearly all splits at the smallest $\alpha$ of every corpus and in
none at the two largest. It errs in the transition region: on DBPedia at
$\alpha=0.02$ it chose the depth-wise test in \res{dbpedia}{0.02}{HLCL}{iutshare}
of splits, and the automatic version needs
\res{dbpedia}{0.02}{HLCL}{effort} against \res{dbpedia}{0.02}{HLCL-wsr}{effort}
for the pooled test alone. The rule is evaluated on the fit split, which is half
the size of the calibration split, so it is biased towards the depth-wise test
near the transition; a rule that accounts for the calibration size would remove
this bias.

\paragraph{Score, closure and per-depth thresholds}
Under a fixed test these components matter in few settings. With the pooled
test on DBPedia at $\alpha=0.02$, the learned score and closure both help
(effort \res{dbpedia}{0.02}{HLCL-wsr}{effort} against
\res{dbpedia}{0.02}{HLCL-vote-wsr}{effort} with the raw vote and
\res{dbpedia}{0.02}{HLCL-flat-wsr}{effort} without closure), and the learned
score saves a few points at larger $\alpha$ on WOS-46985 and with annotator B;
on Amazon, by contrast, the raw vote is cheaper at every $\alpha$ and under
every test, by up to nine points (\res{amazon}{0.02}{HLCL-vote-wsr}{effort}
against \res{amazon}{0.02}{HLCL-wsr}{effort} at $\alpha=0.02$). With the pooled
test, removing closure never lowered effort by more than $0.005$ in our
\stat{s@nsettings} settings. With the depth-wise test it is the other way round:
removing closure lowered effort by more than $0.005$ in 13 of the
\stat{s@nsettings} settings, by up to six points (Amazon at $\alpha=0.15$:
\res{amazon}{0.15}{HLCL-flat-iut}{effort} against
\res{amazon}{0.15}{HLCL-iut}{effort}), because a depth-wise threshold no longer
has to hold for nodes below a rejected parent. Per-depth thresholds matter with
the depth-wise test, where a shared threshold must be strict enough for the
hardest depth (e.g.\ \res{bgc_haiku}{0.05}{HLCL-tied-iut}{effort} against
\res{bgc_haiku}{0.05}{HLCL-iut}{effort} with annotator B at $\alpha=0.05$, and
\res{amazon}{0.05}{HLCL-tied-iut}{effort} against
\res{amazon}{0.05}{HLCL-iut}{effort} on Amazon at $\alpha=0.05$); with the
pooled test they mostly matter at small $\alpha$ (DBPedia at $\alpha=0.02$:
\res{dbpedia}{0.02}{HLCL-tied-wsr}{effort} against
\res{dbpedia}{0.02}{HLCL-wsr}{effort}). We conclude that, in our data, the
gains of \hlcl{} come mainly from the label-level unit of decision, the pooled
certificate and the choice between tests, and not from the learned score or
from closure. Closure is nevertheless required for the output to be a valid path
(Definition~\ref{def:closure}); in our experiments it saves effort under the
pooled test, substantially only on DBPedia at $\alpha=0.02$, and costs a few
points under the depth-wise test.

\paragraph{Objective}
Deploying the certified candidate with the most accepted labels instead of the
cheapest one changes effort by at most a few points at $c_0=0.5$
(Table~\ref{tab:abl} does not show it; the largest change is
\res{amazon}{0.05}{HLCL-maxlab}{effort} against \res{amazon}{0.05}{HLCL}{effort}
on Amazon at $\alpha=0.05$). We did not run the label-maximising variant at
other values of $c_0$.

\subsection{Sensitivity}
\label{sec:exp-sens}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\scriptsize
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}
\caption{Sensitivity of \hlcl{} to the review overhead $c_0$, the calibration
size $n_{\mathrm{cal}}$ and the confidence level $\delta$ (Blurb collection,
annotator A, 100 splits). The last three columns give the effort of the
certified baselines under the same setting; Item-cert.\ here uses the automatic

\label{tab:sens}
\input{tables/sens}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:sens} varies one design parameter at a time on the Blurb
collection.

\paragraph{Review overhead}
The certificate does not depend on $c_0$; only the choice among certified
thresholds does. A larger overhead pushes the deployed rule towards accepting
whole items: at $\alpha=0.05$ the share of fully automatic items rises from
\stat{s@sens@bgc_c0_0@0.05@fullauto} at $c_0=0$ to
\stat{s@sens@bgc_c0_1@0.05@fullauto} at $c_0=1$, while power changes from
\stat{s@sens@bgc_c0_0@0.05@power} to \stat{s@sens@bgc_c0_1@0.05@power}. The
violation share is unchanged, and \hlcl{} remains the cheapest certified method
for every $c_0$.

\paragraph{Calibration size}
With fewer calibration items the certificate becomes more conservative, as
expected: at $\alpha=0.05$ effort rises from \stat{s@sens@bgc@0.05@effort} with
1,200 items to \stat{s@sens@bgc_ncal600@0.05@effort} with 600 and
\stat{s@sens@bgc_ncal300@0.05@effort} with 300. At $\alpha=0.1$ the item-level
rule (automatic variant) loses more: its effort rises from $0.28$ to $0.49$,
against $0.20$ to $0.28$ for \hlcl{}.
With only 300 calibration items and $\alpha=0.05$, HSC is cheaper than \hlcl{};
a plausible reason, which we have not verified, is that its single binomial
certificate on the item-level error needs less data than \hlcl{}'s pooled
label-level one. In these runs the selection rule always chose the pooled test,
because it looks only at the fit split and cannot react to the calibration size.
The violation share stays small throughout.

\paragraph{Confidence level}
Changing $\delta$ from $0.05$ to $0.2$ moves effort by about two points at both
values of $\alpha$, and the violation share tracks $\delta$ as it should
(\stat{s@sens@bgc_delta0.05@0.1@viol}, \stat{s@sens@bgc@0.1@viol} and
\stat{s@sens@bgc_delta0.2@0.1@viol} of splits at $\alpha=0.1$).

\subsection{Second annotator}
\label{sec:exp-annot}

Annotator B is less accurate than annotator A on the Blurb collection at every
depth (Table~\ref{tab:annot}). The guarantee still holds at every $\alpha$, and
\hlcl{} has the lowest mean effort among the certified methods at all four values
of $\alpha$, by one to three points; none of these differences is significant
after the Nadeau--Bengio correction (Table~\ref{tab:main}). The score and the procedure were
applied to annotator B without any change.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Which test when}
The pooled betting test should be the default: it uses the pooled constraint
that operators care about and is sharper when per-depth error rates differ.
The depth-wise test is the fallback for small $\alpha$, where the pooled test
certifies little or nothing. The selection rule makes the switch automatically from the
fit split; the chosen test is recorded in every released result file. Because
the rule does not look at the calibration size, it does not adapt to small
calibration splits (\S\ref{sec:exp-sens}).

\paragraph{High-probability or expected guarantee}
The high-probability guarantee and the expected-FDP guarantee of conformal
labeling bound different functionals, and neither was uniformly cheaper in our
experiments: conformal labeling was slightly cheaper on DBPedia at $\alpha=0.02$
but more expensive at the smallest $\alpha$ on the Blurb collection, and where it
was much cheaper its realised error often exceeded the target. An operator who
re-calibrates often and cares about average quality over many deployments may
prefer the expected form; an operator who must defend the quality of one
released dataset needs the high-probability form. Both can share the node score
and the ancestor-closed rule.

\paragraph{Practical use}
The review step need not be a human; it can be a stronger model, a rule engine
or a domain expert, and the weights $\omega_d$ can reflect the cost of each level. In
a data platform the outcome can be stated as a column policy, i.e.\ which levels
of which taxonomy are written without review at which certified error, and
audited later on a fresh labelled sample.

\paragraph{Limitations}
The guarantee assumes that calibration and deployment items come from the same
distribution; drift in the topic mix invalidates it, as for any calibration-based
method. Items that share a source, such as several messages of one thread, are
not independent; the procedure should then be applied at the level of the
independent unit, as discussed in \cite{perfield2026}. We assume a fixed tree
taxonomy with one gold path per item; multiple gold paths and DAG taxonomies need
a different notion of correctness. The annotator is queried five times per item,
and we have not studied how the score degrades with fewer samples. The effort
model is a stylised default ($c_0$, $\omega_d$) rather than a measured review
time; we show sensitivity to $c_0$ but have not run a timed study. Each corpus
contributes 3,000 items, the deepest taxonomy has four levels, and DBPedia is
easy at the coarse levels, so the DBPedia results mainly test the small-$\alpha$
regime. Finally, the
test-selection rule is a heuristic: it is valid by construction but not optimal.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We studied label-level selective acceptance of hierarchical LLM annotations under
a certified error bound and an explicit reviewing cost. \hlcl{} decides per node,
keeps accepted labels ancestor-closed, certifies per-depth thresholds with a
learn-then-test procedure whose design choices are all fixed on held-out data,
and deploys the cheapest certified threshold. On four public corpora of depth
two to four with two annotators, the share of splits whose realised error
exceeded the target stayed below $\delta=0.1$ (at most
\stat{s@maxviol@HLCL}). The evidence is limited to 3,000 items per corpus,
taxonomies of depth at most four and one second annotator. Under the same certificate, deciding
per label rather than per item accepted substantially more correct labels at
moderate risk. Against the strongest certified baseline in each setting, \hlcl{}
had lower mean effort in most settings, but after correcting for overlapping
splits it is significantly cheaper in \stat{s@wins} and significantly more
expensive in \stat{s@losses}; at very small $\alpha$
hierarchical selective classification, which certifies a different quantity, was
cheaper, and close to the annotator's error rate the item-level rule was as good.
The ablations suggest that the gains come from the unit of decision and the
certificate rather than from the learned score. Code, cached
annotations and per-split results are released.

\section*{Data and code availability}
The four corpora are public: DBPedia classes (licence CC0; Hugging Face
dataset \path{DeveloperOats/DBPedia_Classes}), WOS-46985 (Mendeley Data, dataset
\path{9rw3vkcfy4}), the Blurb Genre Collection (Universit\"at Hamburg,
licence CC BY-NC 4.0) and the Home \& Kitchen metadata of Amazon Reviews 2023
(Hugging Face dataset \path{McAuley-Lab/Amazon-Reviews-2023}). We redistribute
no text from any corpus; users obtain the corpora from their sources under the
providers' terms. The code, the cached LLM responses (labels and stated
confidences only, no source texts), the per-split result files and the scripts
that regenerate every table and figure are available at
\url{https://github.com/wanghongsheng01/hlcl}
(archived with a DOI on Zenodo at acceptance).

\appendix
\section{Proofs}
\label{app:proofs}

\paragraph{Ancestor closure of \eqref{eq:rule}}
If $A_{i,d}=1$ then $\mathbf{1}\{s_{i,e}\ge\lambda_e\}=1$ for every $e\le d$, and
hence $A_{i,e}=1$ for every $e\le d$.

\paragraph{Validity of the depth-wise $p$-value}
Fix $\lambda$ and $d$. The pairs $(A_{i,d},W_{i,d})$ are i.i.d.\ across items,
with $W_{i,d}\le A_{i,d}$. Conditionally on $(A_{1,d},\dots,A_{n,d})$, the
variables $W_{i,d}$ of the items with $A_{i,d}=1$ are independent Bernoulli with
parameter $\Pr(W_{i,d}=1\mid A_{i,d}=1)=q_d$. Hence
$W_d=\sum_i W_{i,d}\mid n_d\sim\Bin(n_d,q_d)$, and under $H_d:q_d>\alpha$ the
binomial tail \eqref{eq:binomial} satisfies $\Pr(p_d\le t\mid n_d)\le t$ for all
$t$, because the $\Bin(n_d,q)$ distribution is stochastically increasing in $q$.
Integrating over $n_d$ gives $\Pr(p_d\le t)\le t$. If $n_d=0$ and $\lambda_d<\infty$ we set $p_d=1$,
which is trivially valid. If $\lambda_d=\infty$ the rule cannot accept at depth
$d$, so $\E[A_d]=0$, depth $d$ does not enter \eqref{eq:weightedavg}, and it is
omitted from the maximum. By \eqref{eq:weightedavg}, $\fdr(\lambda)>\alpha$
implies that $H_d$ holds for some $d$, say $d^\ast$. Then
$\Pr(\max_d p_d\le t)\le\Pr(p_{d^\ast}\le t)\le t$, so $p^{\mathrm{iut}}$ is
valid for $H_\lambda$.

\paragraph{Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:validity}}
Condition on the fit split. The candidates $\lambda_{(1)},\lambda_{(2)},\dots$,
their order and the test statistic are then fixed, and the calibration items are
i.i.d.\ and independent of them, so each $p_{(j)}$ is a valid $p$-value for
$H_{\lambda_{(j)}}$. Fixed-sequence testing rejects $H_{\lambda_{(1)}},\dots,
H_{\lambda_{(J)}}$ where $J$ is the index before the first $p$-value above
$\delta$. Let $j^\ast$ be the smallest index whose null is true. A true null is
rejected only if $J\ge j^\ast$, which requires $p_{(j^\ast)}\le\delta$; hence the
probability of rejecting any true null is at most
$\Pr(p_{(j^\ast)}\le\delta)\le\delta$ \cite{bauer1991multiple}. On the
complementary event, which has probability at least $1-\delta$, every certified
$\lambda$ has $\fdr(\lambda)\le\alpha$ by \eqref{eq:equiv} (a candidate with
$\E[A(\lambda)]=0$ accepts nothing and is harmless). The deployed $\hat\lambda$ is
one of the certified candidates or accepts nothing, which proves
\eqref{eq:guarantee}. The argument is conditional on the fit split and therefore
also holds unconditionally.
